title: Ten Minutes a Day
author: Léxi
desc: Grâce, 24 ans, rate un emploi parce qu'elle ne parle pas anglais. Elle décide d'apprendre dix minutes par jour.

p: Grâce was twenty-four. She had a diploma in accounting, a nice white shirt and a big dream: to work for an international company in Abidjan.
One Monday, she had an interview at a big shipping company in the port. The first questions were in French. Everything went well. She smiled. The manager smiled.
Then a woman came in. "This is Mrs. Johnson, our director from Ghana," said the manager. "She will ask you a few questions in English."
"Good morning, Grâce. Can you tell me about your last job?"
Grâce opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She knew the words *yes*, *no*, *hello*. But that was all. Her face became hot. Her hands became wet.
"I… sorry… my English… no," she said.
Mrs. Johnson smiled kindly. But Grâce knew. She didn't get the job.
On the bus home, Grâce was angry. Angry at herself.
"I don't have time to learn English," she always said. "I don't have money for courses. I'm not good at languages."
At home, her little brother Junior was playing on his phone. "Junior, how do you say *I'm angry* in English?"
"I'm angry," said Junior without looking up. "Easy."
"Where did you learn that?"
"In games. And videos. Everybody knows that."
Grâce sat on her bed. She did the calculation. Every day, she spent at least two hours on her phone. TikTok, WhatsApp, Facebook. Two hours.
"So it's not time I don't have," she said to herself. "It's a decision I didn't make."
That night, Grâce made a rule. Only one. *Ten minutes of English every day. Not one hour. Ten minutes. Even on bad days.*
Ten minutes seemed too small to change anything. But it was small enough to do every day.

Day 1: she learned ten words. Day 2: ten more. Day 5: she listened to a song and understood three sentences. Day 12: she watched a cartoon in English with Junior. Day 20: she was tired and sad, and she wanted to stop. She did only five minutes. But she did them.
She put a calendar on her wall. Every day, a red X. After one month, there were thirty red X's. She didn't want to break the chain.
"Ten minutes is nothing," said her friend Mireille.
"Ten minutes a day is sixty hours a year," answered Grâce.
After three months, Grâce started to think in English sometimes. On the bus, she described what she saw in her head: *a red car, a tired man, a woman selling bananas.*
After four months, she spoke with a tourist at the market. He was lost. She explained the way. He said: "Your English is very good!" She walked home dancing.
After six months, she saw a new job offer. The same shipping company. The same position.
She went to the interview. Mrs. Johnson was there again.
"Good morning. Haven't we met before?"

"Yes, Mrs. Johnson," said Grâce. Her voice was calm. "Six months ago, I couldn't answer your question. So I decided to learn. Ten minutes a day. Today, I can tell you about my last job, and about why I want this one."
Mrs. Johnson put down her pen. "Please," she said with a big smile. "Tell me everything."
Grâce got the job.
On her first day, she put a small paper on her desk. On it, she wrote:
*Big dreams. Small steps. Every day.*
Now, when her friends say "I don't have time", Grâce smiles. She doesn't say anything. She just shows them her old calendar, with one hundred and eighty red X's.
And every evening, on the bus home, she still does her ten minutes. Now she is learning Spanish.
